knowledge_type_note: Restricted deliberately to effects that have been MEASURED. Chess psychology is full of confident folklore, and this record carries only what a study supports.

attributions.note: Established that masters do not search more widely, which is the foundation the later work builds on.

history.notes: A research literature rather than a chess tradition. Several results are recent and thinly replicated.

development.note: De Groot and then Chase and Simon establish pattern recognition and its limits.
Time-pressure studies show quality degrading for strong and weak players alike, more so for the weak.
Large-sample game analysis becomes possible, and engine benchmarks make move quality measurable.

engine_era_note: The engine is what made this field possible: every modern result here depends on scoring human moves against an engine benchmark. Before that, claims about psychology at the board could not be checked at all.

false_positive_traps: None of this is a property of a position and none of it may be attached to a move.
Chess psychology is unusually rich in confident unevidenced claims. This record holds only measured effects and names what it is leaving out.
Population effects do not license statements about an individual player.

typical_plans: Expect to become risk-averse when short of time, and correct for it
Expect to over-reach immediately after an error
Spend attention where errors cluster: unclear positions under time pressure

exceptions: These are tendencies across many games, and any individual game may run against all of them.
limitations: Restricted to measured effects; large parts of what is usually called chess psychology are omitted for lack of evidence, and that omission is deliberate.
Several cited results are recent and have not been widely replicated.
This system cannot observe a player and can only report the general finding.

NO AMBIGUOUS EXAMPLE, and a FEN is not the right kind of evidence for one here. An ambiguous example in this base is a POSITION where the concept is genuinely present and what to conclude from it is unclear - the pattern is on the board and the reading of it is not. This record's subject is not on the board: its `recognition.detectability` is `human-only`, and what it describes is something a player does at the board rather than something the board contains. A position could illustrate the CONSEQUENCE of doing it well or badly, and that is a different claim, and attaching a FEN here would be evidence for the wrong proposition. Recorded rather than filled: tools/depth_report.py still counts this concept as missing the item, and the completion assessment carries the gap.

NO REGISTERED FALSE-POSITIVE CASE, and a FEN is not the right instrument for one here. A case in tests/false_positive_cases.json is a POSITION where the concept's surface pattern is present and the concept is not, replayed as an assertion so the system can be shown declining the error. This record's `recognition.detectability` is `human-only`: what it describes is something a player does rather than something a board contains, so there is no surface pattern for a position to carry and nothing for the system to decline. The conditions this record states are read and answered in `limitations` and in the trap audit instead. Recorded rather than filled: tools/depth_report.py still counts this concept as missing the item.
misconceptions: That masters play mostly on intuition. Time pressure degrades grandmasters and world champions substantially, which it should not if intuition were doing the work.
That masters have better memories. On random positions they do not.
That blunders are random accidents. They concentrate where time pressure and positional ambiguity coincide.

by_level.beginner: When you are short of time you will play more cautiously than you should, especially when you are already worse.
by_level.intermediate: Errors are not random — they cluster where you are short of time AND the position is unclear.
by_level.advanced: Expect risk aversion under time pressure and over-reaching just after a mistake; both are measured tendencies, not character flaws.
by_level.master: Deliberation remains essential at world-champion level, which is not what a purely intuitive account of expertise would predict.

by_depth.short: The measured ways players depart from just playing the position.
by_depth.normal: The parts of chess psychology that have actually been measured: players become more risk-averse when short of time and most so in bad positions, take more risk just after an error, and blunder where low time and an unclear position coincide.
by_depth.deep: Chess writing about psychology is mostly assertion, so this record carries only measured effects. Professionals become more risk-averse as thinking time falls, most strongly in the bad positions where risk is most needed, and take more risk immediately after a mistake. Blunders cluster rather than scatter, concentrating where time pressure and positional ambiguity coincide and amplifying rather than adding. And deliberation remains central even for grandmasters and world champions, whose accuracy degrades under time pressure - which is not what a purely intuitive account of mastery would predict. What is deliberately absent is everything about intimidation, tilt and playing the opponent: possibly real, and not measured here.

explanations.hedge: Only measured effects are recorded, from population studies of many games; they describe tendencies rather than what any player should do in a given position.
explanations.lesson: Know where your errors cluster. That is more useful than resolving to make fewer.

beginner_words: playing it safe when short of time
avoid: play the opponent, not the board

definition_short: The measured, non-obvious ways human decision-making at the board departs from simply choosing the best move.
definition_long:
Chess writing about psychology is mostly assertion. This record holds the parts that have been measured, and says so where a claim is popular but unevidenced.

RISK AVERSION UNDER PRESSURE. Analysis of FIDE World Cups from 2013 to 2023 found that less thinking time consistently pushes professionals towards MORE RISK-AVERSE moves — and that the effect is strongest in bad positions, which is precisely where risk is most needed. The same study found correlational evidence of the opposite tendency after a mistake: players take more risk having just erred. Both are departures from playing the position in front of you.

ERRORS CLUSTER. Blunders are not scattered randomly through a game; they concentrate where low time and an unclear position coincide, and the two amplify each other rather than adding. Knowing WHERE your errors are likely is more useful than resolving to make fewer.

DELIBERATION IS NOT OPTIONAL, EVEN FOR EXPERTS. A study of twenty grandmasters and seven world champions found that time pressure hurt both their speed and their accuracy, and concluded that deliberate calculation remains central at the highest level. The popular picture of the master who simply sees the right move is not what the data shows; what elite players actually do is decide well WHEN to intuit and when to calculate.

PATTERN RECOGNITION IS REAL BUT NARROWER THAN CLAIMED. Masters recall real positions almost perfectly and random ones no better than novices, so the advantage is in meaningful structure rather than memory. And experts search slightly DEEPER than weaker players but not WIDER — the difference is in which moves they look at.

WHAT THIS RECORD DELIBERATELY OMITS: claims about intimidation, playing the opponent rather than the board, tilt, and confidence effects. They may well be real. This base has not found measurements for them, and a system that explains moves has no business asserting them.
